ety.text: The adjective is from Old French liberal, from Latin līberālis (“befitting a freeman”), from līber (“free”); it is attested since the 14th century. The noun is first attested in the 1800s.

senses.d: Generous; permitting liberty; willing to give unsparingly.
ex: He was liberal with his compliments.
Indeed, the Government has been very liberal in the expenditure of public money

senses.d: Ample, abundant; generous in quantity.
ex: Add a liberal sprinkling of salt.
The result was usually that such helpers got a liberal sprinkling of mud over their clothing.

senses.d: Widely open to new ideas, willing to depart from established opinions or conventions; permissive.
ex: Her parents had liberal ideas about child-rearing.

senses.d: Unrestrained, licentious.
Pertaining to a type of education the purpose of which is to cultivate and develop wise, capable and well-rounded people who are thus free of mental constraint and hindrance.

Pertaining to those arts and sciences the study of which is considered to provide general knowledge, as opposed to vocational/occupational, technical or mechanical training; usually found in the phrase "liberal arts".
ex: He had a full education studying the liberal arts.

senses.d: Open to political or social changes and reforms associated with either classical liberalism or "modern liberalism"/progressivism.
One with liberal views, supporting individual liberty (see Wikipedia's article on Liberalism).
Someone with progressive or left-wing views, especially on social and environmental issues.
ex:
And I love Puerto Ricans and Negros
As long as they don't move next door.
So love me, love me, love me, I'm a liberal.

senses.d: A supporter of any of several liberal parties.
One who favors individual voting rights, human and civil rights, and laissez-faire markets (also called "classical liberal"; compare libertarian).
A conservative, especially a liberal conservative.

The noun is derived from liber(ty) + -arian (suffix denoting an advocate of or believer in something). The adjective is derived from the noun. sense development The word was first attested in English in 1789 in William Belsham’s Essays: see the quotation. This was contrasted with necessitarian, in the context of free will, and was not used in the more frequently encountered modern sense. Compare French libertaire (“person with extreme left-wing beliefs, anarchist”), from liberté (“freedom”) + -aire (suffix forming nouns). Libertaire is derived from Latin libertas.

senses.d: One who advocates liberty, either generally or in relation to a specific issue.
ex: civil libertarian
cultural libertarian

senses.d: A believer in the freedom of thinking beings to choose their own destiny (the doctrine of free will) as opposed to those who believe the future is predetermined (the doctrine of necessity).
An antiauthoritarian believer in left-libertarianism, a political doctrine that stresses both individual freedom and social equality, and advocates shared ownership of natural resources.

Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriuslbor. Portuguese -ário Portuguese libertário From Latin lībertātem + Portuguese -ário.

From Middle English librarie, from Anglo-Norman librarie, from Old French librairie, from Latin librarium (“bookcase, chest for books”), from librarius (“concerning books”), from liber (“the inner bark of trees; paper, parchment, book”), probably derived from a Proto-Indo-European base *leub(ʰ)- (“to strip, to peel”). Displaced native Middle English bochous, bokhus (literally “book house”), from Old English bōchūs (compare bookhouse). Romance cognates often mean “bookshop” instead: French librairie, Italian libreria, Spanish librería, Romanian librărie and Portuguese livraria.

senses.d: An institution which holds books and/or other forms of media for use by the public or qualified people often lending them out, as well as providing various other services for its users.
ex: She went to exchange her books at her local library.
When all else fails, give up and go to the library.

senses.d: Any institution that lends out its goods for use by the public or a community.
ex: You can check out a bandsaw from the tool library.

senses.d: A collection of books or other forms of stored information.
ex: A small library of books has been written on the subject.

senses.d: A collection of information or reference materials not in book form.
ex: She has the most impressive record library I've ever seen.

senses.d: A room dedicated to storing books.
A collection of software routines that provide functionality to be incorporated into or used by a computer program.
ex: A static library is much like any other library in that it contains a bunch of code for your application to use.

senses.d: A collection of DNA material from a single organism or relative to a single disease.
The deck or draw pile.
ex: At this phase, most of TCGs only allow players drawing card(s) from a pack which is also called library or deck.

senses.d: The quality of being liberal.
Any political movement founded on the autonomy and personal freedom of the individual, progress and reform, and government by law with the consent of the governed.
ex: Whether some distant cousin really belongs to the extended family of liberalisms is a matter of healthy dispute.

senses.d: An economic ideology in favour of laissez faire and the free market (related to economic liberalism).
ex: But liberalism has no obvious answers to the biggest problems we face: ecological collapse and technological disruption.

senses.d: A school of international relations that emphasises cooperation (such as trade) between polities, as an alternative to power politics, and the geopolitically transformative role of democratisation, as opposed to inherent structural material factors.
